tables.how: Every line of the Controller's Citywide Nonprofit Spending table with fiscal year 2026, as retrieved on 12 November 2026, added up by payee and department: 1,380 payee-and-department rows adding to $2,152,806,662. A row is marked Yes where the case counts a provider-level result as published: for Public Health, at least one programme review of that provider in the contract-monitoring tables given to the Health Commission (2021 to 2024); for Homelessness and Supportive Housing, a contract memo to the Homelessness Oversight Commission with a sentence on whether contract objectives were met, or a count of the provider's beds occupied on the night of the federal count. No other department has published a result by provider that could be found, so every other row is marked No. Rows marked No add to $1,435,717,161, the case's $1,435,717,161 to within a dollar of rounding (67% of the $2,151,836,695 paid by the departments counted); rows marked Yes add to $716,119,534 ($309,504,374 of Public Health's $766,225,213, 40%; $406,615,160 of Homelessness and Supportive Housing's $518,334,466, 78%). $969,966 paid by departments that paid nonprofits under $1 million since fiscal 2019 is left out of the case's count and marked so. The table includes the University of California, which it labels “UCSF”: $364,457,307 in fiscal 2026, $353,020,473 of it from Public Health. All of that is counted as No, although the monitoring tables print 24 reviews of university programmes; so are $7,058,024 paid to three organizations reviewed under a heading the case did not tie to them (see the notes). Counting those reviews would leave $1,075,638,664 (50%) with no published result. In all, $447,210,613 of the money counted went to payees that the organization pages set aside by name as universities, other public bodies or companies (a rule on names, which also catches a few nonprofits whose names begin with “City”; the largest: Regents of The University of California, $334,516,089; Prg-Potrero Properties Llc, $65,000,000; Regents Univ of Ca / SFgh Psychiatry Dpt, $19,039,684); without them $988,506,548 of $1,704,626,082 (58%) has no published result. $175,910,339 of the rows marked No went to providers about which the other of the two departments has published a result. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus documented renames.
tables.limits: This list shows what is published and saved, not what a department knows: departments hold results in systems that are not public. A Yes can rest on one small programme reviewed out of many, or on one count night, and the monitor is the department that pays. Of the university's $353,020,473 from Public Health, $301,112,919 is paid under the contract the table titles “DPH - UC Affiliation Agreement”; the published reviews of university programmes concern mental-health, substance-use and HIV programmes. A payment is money the City sent, not money the payee kept: rent subsidies, child-care subsidies and grants paid onward to others are in these figures. The nonprofit-spending table keeps contracted services only, which is why the table of every payment can differ; a blank in that column means no payment line was found under the payee's name and that department's code. Payees are matched by name.

tables.how: The 60 organizations with the largest totals in the Controller's Citywide Nonprofit Spending table for fiscal 2019 to 2026 (universities and other public bodies are not ranked): $7,114,659,779 together. Each was looked up in every provider-level result on disk recorded by someone else: Public Health's contract monitoring (latest year; missed means a programme scored 1 or 2 of 4, or met under 80% of contracted objectives), the homelessness department's memo sentences, beds occupied on the federal count night against the City's own occupancy target, federal building inspections and State adult day health attendance (the last two are independent but have no City target). Where a monitor has recorded a result against the contract, that decides the verdict; the count-night occupancy decides it only when no monitor result is published. The organization's own count is the largest count of people on its latest tax return, found by text search, shown for contrast only. 16 carry the verdict “independent measure, target missed” ($2,439,053,037); 14 carry the verdict “independent measure, target met” ($1,953,432,471); 5 carry the verdict “independent measure, no target” ($537,564,766); 15 carry the verdict “only its own reports” ($1,380,493,114); 10 carry the verdict “no result on record” ($804,116,391). The last two groups are 25 organizations paid $2,184,609,505 (31% of the money). Ranked instead on the table of every payment less loans, 4 others would be among the 60 (Delta Dental Plan of California, $508,963,773; Homebridge Inc, $241,154,367; SF New Deal, $75,082,228; Union Square Business Improvmnt District, $52,876,745) in place of Central City Hospitality House; Bayview Hunters Pt Multipurpose Sr Svc; Bay Area Legal Aid; Project Open Hand. The lists of reviews, memos and outside counts in this file give the single records behind each verdict.
tables.limits: A verdict describes what is published, not how well an organization works. “Target met” or “missed” usually rests on one programme or one count night out of everything the organization does, and the monitors are the departments that fund it. For several organizations the latest published review covers a pandemic year, when sites were closed and objectives were widely missed. “Only its own reports” and “no result on record” mean no outside result was found on disk: departments hold results in systems that are not public, notably for children's, early-childhood, human-services, workforce and housing grants. A missed target is not misconduct. Organizations are matched by name. The totals are payments, including money an organization pays onward to others, and come from the nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only.

tables.how: Count-night occupancy: every provider with 60 or more shelter, transitional, safe-haven or supportive-housing beds in San Francisco's federal Housing Inventory Count for January 2025, with the beds the count found occupied (31 providers; 23 could be tied to a City payee by name). The City's own target for occupancy of site-based supportive housing in fiscal 2025 is the yardstick the verdicts use. Building inspections: the latest federal inspection score of each subsidised building whose owner or manager is a City-paid organization, among the 60 lowest-scoring of 119 buildings that the analysis keeps. Adult day health: average daily attendance against licensed capacity in the State's monthly centre file, for centres run by a City-paid organization.
tables.limits: These are counts of one night, one visit or one centre, kept for federal or State purposes and not as a test of a City contract. Beds can be empty on the count night because they are being turned over or held offline. An inspection score reflects one visit and the scoring method changed in 2023. Buildings and providers are tied to City payees by name only, and a building that scored well enough to fall outside the lowest-scoring group the analysis keeps is not listed, so an organization can have inspected buildings and none here. Federal and State clinic reports are filed by the organization itself and are not counted as outside records.

tables.how: Every measure in the Controller's Citywide Performance Metrics dataset that concerns a service nonprofits mostly deliver (65 measures; the next two lists show all of them). Each year in which the full-year result missed the target was paired with the target published for the following fiscal year, including targets already published for fiscal 2026 to 2028. Of 174 such missed years the next target was easier 52 times (30%), the same 102 times and harder 20 times; after a year in which the target was met it was eased 15 times in 224 (7%). A target counts as easier when it moved down where higher is better, or up where lower is better. In 21 of the 52 rows the new target was at or below the result of the missed year. 46 rows fall outside fiscal 2020 and 2021. The 52 rows concern 29 measures.
tables.limits: These are the City's own figures about whole programmes, reported by each department to the Controller. They are not about any one organization: the dataset names no provider, so no nonprofit can be named on these rows. A missed target can mean the target was set too high, that need grew faster than money, or that the pandemic closed services. Lowering a target after a miss can be honest planning: a budget cut, the end of pandemic money or a change in how a measure is counted are all good reasons to expect less, and the dataset records none of these reasons. Nothing here shows that a target was eased to hide a miss. Measures that were dropped from the dataset altogether cannot be seen.

tables.how: Every row of the Controller's Citywide Performance Metrics dataset was read. Kept: the 65 measures about homelessness, housing placement, shelter, behavioural health and treatment, workforce, children and youth, early childhood, meals and community services for older people, re-entry services and street cleaning, in each year that has both a target and a full-year result: 399 measure-years, of which 225 (56%) met the target. In fiscal 2025, 37 of 65 did. Through fiscal 2019, 74 of 107 measure-years met the target (69.2%); from fiscal 2022 on, 115 of 215 (53.5%, which the case prints as 54%). A year counts as met when the result reached the target: at or above it where higher is better, at or below it where lower is better. Measures of caseload, whose targets are forecasts, are left out.
tables.limits: These are the City's own figures about whole programmes, reported by each department to the Controller. They are not about any one organization: the dataset names no provider, so no nonprofit can be named on these rows. A missed target can mean the target was set too high, that need grew faster than money, or that the pandemic closed services. The dataset keeps only measures that are still current, so a measure retired before 2026 is absent; the homelessness department replaced all of its measures in fiscal 2023, which is why its series are short. Street cleaning is done mostly by City crews. Which measures concern services nonprofits deliver, and which direction is better, were decided measure by measure in the analysis.

tables.how: Each programme row in the contract-compliance tables and monitoring reports attached to Health Commission contract items from 2021 to 2024, read from the text of each paper; a review tabled at more than one meeting is kept once: 240 reviews. 236 give a share of contracted objectives met: 89 (38%) met every objective and 72 met under 80%. 61 carry an overall score, 6 of them 1 or 2 on the 4-point scale. The case says the 240 reviews are of 33 nonprofits. 190 of the reviews are tied to those 33; 24 are of University of California programmes, 8 are under three headings that the case did not tie to a payee, 12 have a heading cut off in the paper's text and 6 are of other providers not in the nonprofit-spending table. The third column says which. 6 reviews are counted twice, once from a single monitoring report and once from the row of a summary table that carries the same figures, so the 240 rows are 234 separate reviews; 1 of the 6 scored 1 or 2 is such a repeat.
tables.limits: The scores are recorded by the department that pays the provider, not by an outside body, and are published only for contracts that came before the commission in these years; most contracts have no published score. Scoring was suspended for fiscal 2020 and 2021 because of the pandemic, when sites were closed and objectives were widely missed. The tables are read by rule from the text of each paper: a figure can be misread and a heading cut off, so the link governs. A low share of objectives on one programme says little about the rest of a provider's work.

tables.how: Every contract memo in the Homelessness Oversight Commission's meeting papers saved on disk whose performance history could be read: 108 memos. In each, the first sentence that mentions objectives was picked out and sorted by its wording: 8 say objectives were met, 7 say not all were met or reported, 2 mention objectives without a clear result, and 91 have no such sentence. None gives the figure achieved against any objective. A provider and programme can come before the commission more than once, and a later memo can repeat an earlier sentence: the 108 memos concern 95 provider-and-programme pairs, and the 17 with a sentence concern 15.
tables.limits: A memo with no sentence about objectives usually reports the provider's fiscal and programme monitoring in other words (findings made and resolved), so it is not silent on performance; it is silent on results against the contract's objectives. The sentences are sorted by key words, which can misread a careful sentence: read the memo. The department's monitor is the department that pays the provider.

Providers with no City payee tied to them (the University of California among them) are listed without money.
tables.limits: A rise in payments after a weak review is not a reward for it. Reviews are completed months after the fiscal year ends, so the following year's budget was usually fixed first; most rises are cost-of-living increases or new programmes unrelated to the one reviewed; and one weak programme among many says little about the rest. In the pandemic years objectives were often missed because sites were closed. The payment is for everything the department bought from the provider, not for the programme reviewed. Whether the weak programme itself was corrected is rarely in the published papers.

tables.how: Objectives were taken by the download step from 400 documents: Board of Supervisors contract attachments, homelessness and human-services commission packets, and Public Health's objectives documents. Rows that name one organization were kept once each (the same opening words count once); lines about units of service and standard clauses were dropped. That leaves 2,836 objectives for 40 organizations, 1,283 with a percentage target; the next list gives every one. A further 1,279 Public Health objectives apply to every contractor of a given kind and are not counted against any organization. The recorded result is the latest Public Health review or homelessness memo sentence for the organization in the lists above, or its beds occupied on the federal count night. For 16 organizations none was found: they were paid $430,960,861 in fiscal 2026 (the case's $431.0 million). City money here is the Controller's table of every payment, less the lines it labels as loans; the nonprofit-spending table's figure is beside it. The case calls these the 40 most-paid nonprofits: 40 of them are among the 40 paid most in the nonprofit-spending table since fiscal 2019 and 38 among the 40 paid most in the table of every payment; the two rank columns show where each stands.
tables.limits: The objectives were extracted by rule: some rows are headings or fragments, the organization is sometimes taken from the nearest name on the page, and an objective can recur in an amendment in slightly different words, so the counts are approximate. Departments collect results against these objectives in their own systems; what is missing is publication, not necessarily measurement. The fiscal 2026 figure includes money the organization pays onward to others: child-care subsidies, rent subsidies and the like are real City payments but not payment for the organization's own work. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment. For Children's Council of San Francisco, $35.7 million printed under fiscal 2025 was issued in June 2024 by its voucher numbers; that moves neither its fiscal 2026 figure nor its eight-year total here. Organizations that contract only with Public Health show few objectives because their contracts point to the department-wide documents.

tables.limits: Each area reports its own figures to the federal government from its own data system, under shared rules; no outside body recounts them. The federal grant is a small part of what San Francisco spends, so dollars per exit compare federal money only. The share depends on which programmes enter records: San Francisco's count of people leaving rose several-fold after 2019 as shelters joined the system, which lowers the share without any change on the ground. Areas with cheaper housing place people more easily. The figures are for whole systems and name no provider.

tables.how: Every line of the Controller's Citywide Nonprofit Spending table for the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing, added up by payee and fiscal year: fiscal 2019 $158,857,930 (56 payees); fiscal 2020 $181,494,761 (57 payees); fiscal 2021 $274,351,643 (64 payees); fiscal 2022 $337,930,835 (68 payees); fiscal 2023 $361,090,416 (71 payees); fiscal 2024 $406,040,966 (74 payees); fiscal 2025 $489,430,335 (77 payees); fiscal 2026 $518,334,466 (81 payees). These yearly sums are the money in the previous list. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use.
tables.limits: A payment is money the department sent, not money the payee kept: rent subsidies and money paid onward to other providers are in these figures, and rent the City pays directly to landlords is not. The nonprofit-spending table keeps contracted services only, which is why the table of every payment can differ; a blank there means no payment line was found under the payee's name and the department's code. The fiscal year is the one printed on the payment.

tables.how: The audits, assessments and grand-jury reports saved on disk that deal with programme results: 17 reports issued from 2018 to 2026. Each row restates the conclusion in plain words and gives one quotation of at most twelve words, which the analysis checked is present word for word in the saved text of the report.
tables.limits: One sentence cannot carry a whole report, and most of these reports also record progress and the department's reply. Several are years old and the departments have since changed their contracts and measures. Grand-jury reports are the work of citizen volunteers, not professional auditors. The State Auditor's report on homelessness funding examined the State and two other cities, not San Francisco. None of the reports found that a programme does not work.
